paragraphs.heading: Where land meets ocean
paragraphs.text: A marine coastal ecosystem is a marine ecosystem found where the land meets the ocean. The world has about 620,000 kilometres of coastline. Coastal habitats reach out to the edges of the continental shelves and take up about 7 percent of the ocean's surface area. They include many very different kinds of habitat, each with its own characteristics and mix of species. They are marked by high levels of biodiversity and productivity.

paragraphs.heading: Estuaries, salt marshes and mangroves
paragraphs.text: Estuaries are areas where freshwater rivers meet the ocean's salt water, making a home for a wide variety of species, among them fish, shellfish and birds. Salt marshes are coastal wetlands that thrive on low-energy shorelines, in temperate areas and at high latitudes. Their salt-tolerant plants, such as cordgrass and marsh elder, give many species of fish and shellfish important nursery areas. Mangrove forests survive on tropical or subtropical coasts, in the intertidal zones. Their salt-tolerant trees protect habitat for many marine species, crabs, shrimp and fish among them.

paragraphs.heading: Coral reefs and seagrass meadows
paragraphs.text: Coral reefs and seagrass meadows are both found in warm, shallow coastal waters. The reefs thrive in waters poor in nutrients, on high-energy shorelines stirred by waves. They are made of colonies of tiny animals called coral polyps, which secrete hard skeletons of calcium carbonate. The skeletons build up over time into complex and varied underwater structures, which rank among the most biodiverse ecosystems on the planet. Seagrass meadows, which can lie next to coral reefs, are underwater grasslands of marine flowering plants. They give nursery habitat and food to many fish species, to crabs and sea turtles, and to dugongs.

paragraphs.heading: Kelp forests
paragraphs.text: In slightly deeper waters are kelp forests, found in cold, nutrient-rich waters, mainly in temperate regions. Kelp is a large brown alga, a type of seaweed that grows several meters tall and forms dense, complex underwater forests. These forests are important habitat for many fish species, sea otters and sea urchins.

paragraphs.heading: Between the tides
paragraphs.text: Intertidal zones are the areas that are exposed to air at low tide and covered by salt water at high tide. The intertidal zone has four physical divisions, each with its own characteristics and wildlife. They are the spray zone, the high intertidal zone, the middle intertidal zone and the low intertidal zone. The spray zone is a damp area, submerged only under high tides or storms.

paragraphs.heading: What these habitats do for people
paragraphs.text: These ecosystems do a great deal for people, directly and indirectly. They cycle nutrients and elements and purify water by filtering out pollutants. They lock away carbon, a cushion against climate change. They protect coasts by softening the impacts of storms, cutting coastal erosion and moderating extreme events. Commercial fisheries get essential nurseries and fishing grounds from them. They also offer recreation and support tourism.

paragraphs.heading: Under pressure
paragraphs.text: Coastal ecosystems are vulnerable to disturbances such as pollution, overfishing and coastal development. Climate change is affecting them through sea level rise, ocean acidification, and more frequent and more intense storms. According to recent studies, more than half of all people in the world live within 200km or so of a coastline. Some conservation efforts are underway, such as setting up marine protected areas and developing sustainable fishing practices. The United Nations has declared 2021–2030 the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, yet coastal ecosystems are not getting appropriate attention in restoration.
